hints: Focus on what is actually made in every neutralisation, no matter which acid or alkali you use.
Remember that some acids like $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and some alkalis like $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ can make more than one mole of water per mole of reactant.
Think about which amount must be fixed at one mole to give a fair, consistent value for all acids and alkalis.
walkthrough:
**Recall what neutralisation always does**

Think simply first. Every acid-alkali reaction makes water from $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$.

$$\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**See why one mole of acid is not fixed**

Not all acids are the same. A diprotic acid like $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives two moles of $\text{H}^+$ per mole, so it makes two moles of water.

So defining by one mole of acid would give double the energy for $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ compared to $\text{HCl}$. That is not standard or fair.

**See why one mole of alkali is not fixed**

The same problem happens with alkalis. One mole of $\text{NaOH}$ makes one mole of water, but one mole of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ makes two moles of water.

So defining by one mole of alkali also changes the amount of reaction.

**Fix the definition on water**

To keep it consistent, we fix the product. Standard enthalpy of neutralisation is always per one mole of water formed under standard conditions, with all substances aqueous except water.

This leads directly to the correct definition.

options.A: Incorrect. One mole of acid does not always make one mole of water. For example, one mole of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)$ makes two moles of water, so this definition would not be consistent.
options.B: Incorrect. One mole of alkali does not always make one mole of water. For example, one mole of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq)$ makes two moles of water, so this definition would vary between alkalis.
options.C: Incorrect. This is still based on moles of acid and alkali, not on moles of water formed. It fails for diprotic acids or dibasic alkalis and is a common trap that sounds more precise but is still wrong.
options.D: Correct. This is the exact standard definition. By stating per one mole of water produced from aqueous acid plus aqueous alkali, the value is always about $-57.3$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ for strong acid-strong base and is comparable for all reactions.
